You should always select a design most appropriate for your situation. OOP is sometimes useful, but in other situations it is not. Trying to force it on absolutely everything, just on principle alone, is counter productive.

Moreover, although OOP - or other programming paradigms (did I just use that word in a sentence? :-) ) - may allow one to express a good design neatly, it is not going to make bad ideas and lousy designs better. Don't use it as a crutch.
You know, that's completely useless advice. How do you know when OOP is appropriate?
I don't think there is a general way to tell in general. You need to think about it on a case by case basis.

I think it's a solid, practical approach to structuring large programs. Don't let it (or any other aspect of software design) become a religion or apply it without thinking, but it's definitely useful.

I think Functional, Procedural, and Object-oriented programming all have their places. It really depends on the project. I would say that OOP has more flexibility to fill gaps, but it's not the best idea in all situations.

I don't like it,

When done well, it is great, but it is not easy to get it right. Java did not get it right, and that is the only example of an OOP language that most people are familiar with. Similarly, it is difficult to get right in C++, but it does offer the possibility. (Though one might opine that anything is difficult in C++; certainly almost anything is possible.)

When done right, it is almost indistinguishable from typed functional programming. And therein lies its strength: It allows an easy and intuitive (if almost always inefficient) approach to structured programming in imperative language. It is also its great weakness: It easily allows people to write bad programs and hide the mess behind data encapsulation and polymorphism.

In python, you probably want to use object oriented programming to handle complexity, code reuse and "generic programming". However, I consider it a bad habit to approach problems with an object oriented mindset.

I use it where I can't avoid it.

Just talking about OO, if you're a beginner, the thing is not to think too quickly about classes, let them develop organically in the "mess of code" you're writing

If you have a program with code which looks as though it can be split out into different classes, there might not be a need to do it. A class with one method? Might as well leave the code mixed in with something else and a comment as to why the code is there and not in its own class.

Not sure if the code you're writing belongs in the current class or a new class, create a struct and see how that develops. Again, commenting your code with your intentions.

Of course, when writing tests for your code, if it's difficult to write the tests then it might be worth spltting your program into the natural classes that you see.

This is a really good book about OO. It's written in Ruby but the techniques can obviously be used in Python. I've read a lot of OO books and this is by far the best I've read.

I quite like OO programmming but I don't get hung up on it and take a lazy, organic approach to it all.

I love object oriented programming and use it nearly everywhere. It's definitely not perfect, but it's a practice that always has and will continue to evolve (until something better comes along?). In my experience, OOP offers a few major benefits that are more difficult to obtain when using procedural programming. Keep in mind that poor programming using OOP techniques can make life a living hell and can completely negate all of these benefits.

  1. Abstraction - OOP is great for abstracting out commonly used functionality and patterns. Interfaces and abstractions are GREAT ways of ensuring that other developers follow a predefined structure for their objects, or at least implement the bare minimum of functionality required for an object to perform a particular task.

  2. Reusability - Objects can be highly reusable. You can move a general object from project to project then extend it for project-specific needs. This can save a huge amount of work when creating lots of similar projects.

  3. Organization - When programmed clearly and naming conventions are followed, objects can be almost self-documenting. Without even basic comments or annotations, much object code and structure can be readily understood without much effort.

  4. Maintainability - Objects are generally more maintainable than procedural code. This is more anecdotal, but I've found that when onboarding new developers, procedural code requires more review time for a developer to become productive than object oriented code. It's also easier to get back into developing a large project after years away.

All this being said, choose what works best for you and your situation. Since I'm usually doing larger projects, I tend to try an object oriented design approach first, then if there are problems or major roadblocks, look for other avenues of approach.

One common thing I see is that people who understand programming with functions (thanks, Logo!) simply use object classes as a replacement for function libraries, and they never fully grasp the value of storing data in object properties. They then rely on global variables and the return values from methods to control the program flow. Objects were developed from the need to combine structured data with functions specific to that structure, and if you have an object that doesn't have both properties and methods then you aren't doing OO.

I like it, personally. I feel like it's a useful tool to have when you need to use it. Programming paradigms and choices to make are really just tools to use to solve problems. OO is really great for some of these problems, less so for others. I use it often, I find it to be a useful way to design programs and applications. That being said, OO is often done wrong and I feel like many people try to force OO where oftentimes you might not want to use it.

On that note, I hate working with it half the time. Instead of being neat, structured, and easily organized, most of the time it just ends up being messy, obtuse, code is all over the place, data types are scattered about everywhere, and things become way more complicated than they should be otherwise.

It could be good as a level of variable scope that's intermediate between global and local to a function. If you have multiple functions all operating on the same data a class could be a good way to group that data.

Object-oriented programming also implies run-time polymorphism, which isn't necessary. Occasionally it may make your code slightly shorter, but it's overused, and I doubt that it's worth it.

Another meaning of OOP is inheritance. I don't think that's a good language feature.

OOP was a fad and most of what was said about it was rubbish. It gave people the idea that they should have class hierarchies and polymorphism everywhere in order to be clean and extensible. In fact, it's the skill of the programmer to use as little or as much abstraction and indirection as needed to make the code clear, debuggable and extensible for real and expected purposes.

Here's a page that demonstrates why C++ sucks: http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_60_0/libs/geometry/doc/html/geometry/design.html

I like it a lot, even though I started out as an assembler programmer. OOP makes it easier for me to keep an overview.

In practice it does tend to become more work for the same solution, because it has more overhead. Then again, once it's done, reuse is easier, so it can be much faster when reuse is possible (which sadly, doesn't happen as often as you'd like). I still prefer it though, but perhaps that's because it just clicks with the way my brain works.

The biggest issue with it is how in practice reuse often comes with issues. Existing components tend to need other existing components, which very often results in different components requiring conflicting versions of other components. Even with things like OSGi, which try to be a solution to that problem, it's merely a patch because it can never be perfect (even when you can use different versions, you may still need to translate the objects). This problem is more prevalent in object oriented programming than with functional or procedural. On the other hand, this is actually an issue arising from big upside of OOP: the easier reuse. It's just not as easy as it may seem in theory, but especially when you can just "click" on major components it can often simplify work massively.
